{{Short description|American biologist (1927–2021)}}
[[File:Dick Estes.jpg|thumb]]
'''Richard Despard Estes''' (December 26, 1927 - December 6, 2021) was an American [[Ethology|ethologist]]<ref>{{Cite web|author=Abraham, Curtis|url=https://theecologist.org/2019/nov/15/insights-serengeti-ecosystem|title=Insights into the Serengeti ecosystem|work=[[The Ecologist]]|date=15 November 2019|access-date=1 August 2026}}</ref> and [[biologist]] specialising in the [[ethology|behaviour]] of [[mammal]]s in mainland [[Africa]]. He was particularly interested in studying [[wildebeest]]. This interest led Rod East, the former co-chair of the Antelope Specialist Group of the IUCN-[[World Conservation Union]], to dub him the 'Guru of Gnu.'<ref>{{Cite web|url= http://www.nwf.org/News-and-Magazines/National-Wildlife/Animals/Archives/2005/The-Guru-of-Gnu.aspx |title= The Guru of Gnu |last= Boroughs |first= Don |date= February 1, 2005 |publisher= National Wildlife Federation |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120204080737/http://www.nwf.org/News-and-Magazines/National-Wildlife/Animals/Archives/2005/The-Guru-of-Gnu.aspx|archive-date= February 4, 2012 |url-status=live}}</ref> It has been suggested that Estes is responsible for most of the world's knowledge of wildebeest behaviour.<ref>Don Boroughs, [https://web.archive.org/web/20040816042821/http://www.bbc.co.uk/nature/animals/features/353feature1.shtml 'Guru of the Gnus,'] [[BBC Wildlife]] magazine, July 2004.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Richard Despard Estes |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/ledgertranscript/name/richard-estes-obituary?id=31885911 |publisher=Monadnock Ledger-Transcript |access-date=13 January 2022}}</ref>

Estes chose to study wildebeest because he thought they were 'the most interesting' animals he knew, particularly in their [[Rut (mammalian reproduction)|rutting]] behaviour. He obtained his [[doctorate]] in the early 1960s with a thesis on the wildebeest of the [[Ngorongoro Crater]], in which he advanced the theory that the females' [[estrus]] was triggered by the rumbling 'love call' of the males. Estes has spent most of the ensuing 40 years doing field work in Africa. In 2004 he began a project in cooperation with the [[Smithsonian Institution]] to test his early theory using new advances in [[molecular]] [[chemistry]].

Estes has written two guides for travellers to Africa, ''The Behavior Guide to African Mammals'' (considered the standard reference of its kind) and ''The Safari Companion.''

Estes lived in [[Peterborough, New Hampshire]] until his death in 2021.<ref>{{cite book |title= |id= {{ASIN|1890132446|country=uk}}}}{{title missing|date=May 2022}}</ref>
